headline: Google surges nearly 6% on blowout AI results, dragging the whole portfolio higher — a great day on the ASX and a cracking night on Wall Street.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: GOOG had a huge night — up nearly 6% last night after Alphabet reported blowout quarterly results, with Google Cloud growing 103% and generative AI demand accelerating. The market re-rated the stock sharply upward as investors realised AI is already driving real revenue, not just hype.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI rode the AI wave hard today, up 4.4% at today's close. Semiconductor and AI stocks had their biggest single-day rebound in over 18 months, and this ETF — packed with AI-exposed companies — was a direct beneficiary.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE closed up 3.5% today in a broad risk-on session. Emerging market stocks bounced strongly alongside global equities, helped by a weaker US dollar and improved sentiment around global growth.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS closed up 2.8% today, tracking the massive rally on Wall Street last night where the NASDAQ jumped 6.5% and the S&P 500 rose 4.7%. This ETF gives you broad US market exposure, so it captured the full force of that rebound.

movers.name: BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF
movers.note: DHHF gained 2.2% today, lifted by strong performances across its global equity holdings — particularly US and tech-heavy positions that benefited from last night's Wall Street surge.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG rose 2% at today's close, carried higher by its global equity exposure. The Wall Street AI-led rally flowed through to this diversified fund's international holdings.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT added 1.65% last night — a solid but quieter session for Microsoft compared to Alphabet's fireworks. The stock continues to benefit from broader AI tailwinds and its Azure cloud business, though it wasn't the catalyst last night.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS dipped a touch today, down 0.7%. The story here remains the same — lithium prices are still struggling to recover despite booming EV demand in China, partly because supply has outpaced demand. China's electric truck boom hasn't been enough to shift the needle on lithium prices.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO was essentially flat last night, down 0.3%. No major news specific to the company — the GTA 6 hacker was released from custody in the UK with a warning, but that's unlikely to affect the investment thesis. The market is simply waiting on GTA 6 news.

watch_today.title: GOOG surges 6% — AI is paying off for Alphabet
watch_today.detail: Google Cloud grew 103% and generative AI demand is driving real revenue, not just promises. This is exactly the long-term thesis playing out. Last night's jump takes GOOG to $279.53 USD — still slightly below your average buy-in cost in AUD terms, but the gap is closing. No reason to sell; the story is getting stronger.

watch_today.title: GXAI up 4.4% — AI stocks rebounding hard
watch_today.detail: Your Global X AI ETF had a strong day, up 4.4% to $15.22. Despite today's bounce, you're still sitting at a -19% loss on this position. The underlying thesis (AI infrastructure spending) is intact — if anything, Alphabet's Cloud results reinforce it. Long-term hold; don't panic-sell into what looks like a turning point.

watch_today.title: PLS continues to drift — lithium price remains the problem
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals fell another 0.7% today and you're now down nearly 60% on this position. The issue is structural: lithium supply has flooded the market faster than EV demand can absorb it. China's electric truck boom hasn't been enough. No sign yet of a price floor. This is the one position worth keeping a close eye on — if the investment thesis (a lithium price recovery) is broken, that's worth reviewing.

watch_today.title: Wall Street had a massive night — S&P up 4.7%, NASDAQ up 6.5%
watch_today.detail: Last night's US session was one of the biggest single-day rallies in over a year, driven largely by Alphabet's blowout results and a broader AI rebound. This flowed through to the ASX today (up 1.8%) and lifted almost every holding in your portfolio. US markets open again tonight — worth watching to see if the momentum holds or gives back some gains.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cuts could come as early as June — good news for growth assets
watch_today.detail: Multiple economists and market commentators are now tipping the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) could start cutting interest rates from June 2026. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned of unemployment rising above 5% and tougher economic conditions ahead. Lower rates are generally good for growth-oriented ETFs like VDHG and VTS — they make future earnings more valuable and reduce competition from savings accounts.

watch_today.title: Three tankers ablaze in Strait of Hormuz — oil markets on watch
watch_today.detail: Iran's Revolutionary Guard reports three oil tankers are on fire in the Strait of Hormuz — a critical chokepoint for global oil supply. Oil is barely moving right now ($80/barrel, almost flat), but if the conflict escalates, an oil price spike would flow through to inflation and potentially delay central bank rate cuts worldwide. Worth keeping an eye on.

world.summary: The Middle East is flaring up again with attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran is showing off military muscle, global flight routes continue to be disrupted, and the aftermath of the US midterms is reshaping international alliances. Carlos Alcaraz also made history in tennis.

stories.title: Three oil tankers ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz
stories.why_it_matters: Iran's Revolutionary Guard confirmed three tankers are on fire in the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway that roughly 20% of the world's oil passes through every day. Any sustained disruption here sends oil prices sharply higher, which flows through to petrol prices and inflation globally. Oil markets are barely reacting yet ($80/barrel, essentially flat), suggesting traders think this may be contained — but the situation is live and bears watching.

stories.title: Iran unveils new missile launcher and touts military capabilities
stories.why_it_matters: Iran publicly unveiled a new missile launcher system, with commanders talking up their readiness for a potential conflict with the US. This is saber-rattling at a moment of heightened regional tension following the tanker attacks. The timing matters — it signals Iran is not backing down and is willing to publicly display its military capabilities, raising the stakes in the Middle East standoff.

stories.title: Dubai and Middle East flight disruptions continue as Gulf states report more attacks
stories.why_it_matters: Flight cancellations and route suspensions are continuing across the Gulf region as attacks on civilian and commercial infrastructure mount. If you're travelling through Dubai or any Middle Eastern hub in the coming weeks, check your airline's status. Beyond travel disruption, the broader economic impact — on tourism, trade, and insurance premiums — is starting to add up across the region.

stories.title: US midterms aftermath: What's next for global partnerships?
stories.why_it_matters: Political analysts are now dissecting what the US midterm results mean for America's role in the world — from trade deals and defence alliances to climate commitments and international institutions. The Trump administration's approach has already rattled traditional partnerships, and the midterms will shape how much political room the White House has to push its foreign policy agenda into 2027.

stories.title: Carlos Alcaraz joins Agassi, Federer and Djokovic in Grand Slam history
stories.why_it_matters: Carlos Alcaraz has become only the fourth man in tennis history to win all four Grand Slams AND the ATP Finals in his career, joining Andre Agassi, Roger Federer, and Novak Djokovic. At just 23, he's achieved something that eluded most of the sport's legends. This is a genuine milestone in the sport's history.

markets.summary: Wall Street had a barnstormer last night — the NASDAQ rocketed 6.5% and the S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, powered by Alphabet's blowout AI results and a massive rebound in tech and semiconductor stocks. The ASX followed suit today, closing up 1.8%. Gold eased off slightly, oil is basically flat, and the Aussie dollar is holding around 66 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today, closing up 1.8% — the global AI rally flowed through to Australian-listed tech and diversified funds.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: One of the biggest single-session gains in over a year last night — Alphabet's AI earnings were the trigger.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Massive night for tech last night — semiconductor and AI stocks had their best day in 18+ months.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Barely moved despite the tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz — markets aren't pricing in an escalation yet.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold slipped about 1% — a classic pattern when risk appetite surges and investors move out of safe-haven assets into equities.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially flat, hovering around 66.3 US cents.

politics.summary: It's a big week in Australian politics — Treasurer Chalmers is warning of tougher times ahead, the RBA rate cut conversation is heating up, new online safety laws are progressing, and the Solomon Islands has scrapped its security deal with China in a win for Australian diplomacy. Victoria also heads to the polls.

stories.title: Chalmers warns unemployment will top 5% and 'things will get harder'
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has told Australians to brace for unemployment rising above 5% — up from current levels — and says 'things might get a bit harder' ahead of the mid-year budget update. He stopped short of predicting a recession, but the language is notably cautious. This is important for everyday Aussies: more people out of work means less spending, potentially softer house prices, and more pressure on the government's budget bottom line.

stories.title: RBA rate cuts could start as early as June — economy deteriorating
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple major banks and economists are now forecasting the RBA (Reserve Bank) could begin cutting interest rates from June this year, with the economy showing signs of deterioration. ANZ is a bit more cautious, tipping June 2027. For mortgage holders, rate cuts mean lower repayments — potentially hundreds of dollars a month. For investors, lower rates generally support higher share prices and make growth assets more attractive. Australia's bond market is already pricing this in, with government bonds rallying.

stories.title: Solomon Islands scraps security agreement with China — big win for Australia
stories.why_it_matters: The Solomon Islands has torn up its security deal with China — the agreement that sent shockwaves through the Pacific when it was signed in 2022. This is a significant diplomatic win for Australia, which has spent years trying to limit Chinese military influence in the Pacific. It signals that Australian diplomatic engagement (and likely financial aid) has been effective in keeping the region within Australia's traditional sphere of influence.

stories.title: New digital safety laws: Labor and Greens strike deal on 'duty of care' for tech giants
stories.why_it_matters: Labor and the Greens have struck a deal on new online safety laws that would require tech giants like Meta, TikTok, and YouTube to actively address addictive design features — including 'doomscrolling' (the endless scroll that keeps you hooked on a feed). Companies that design their platforms to be addictive could face legal liability. Critics say it threatens free speech; supporters say it protects users, especially kids. The laws are expected to pass with Greens support.

stories.title: New defence laws spark civil liberties debate — secret rules and protest rights
stories.why_it_matters: New defence legislation allows the government to create security rules that can be kept secret from the public — drawing fierce criticism from Amnesty International, constitutional law experts, and civil liberties groups. Experts have called the bill 'lazy and irresponsible,' warning it could be used to restrict peaceful protest. The government says critics are 'jumping at shadows.' This is a live debate about the balance between national security and democratic rights in Australia.

ai.summary: AI governance is dominating the headlines today — from Australian senators pushing for tougher laws, to US governors calling for aligned regulation, to China's Ant Group open-sourcing a medical AI model. Meanwhile, benchmark results comparing GPT, Claude, and Gemini have landed.

stories.title: Senator Pocock calls for tougher AI laws and a data centre levy
stories.why_it_matters: ACT Senator David Pocock is pushing for Australia to introduce stricter AI laws and a levy on data centres — the massive electricity-hungry buildings that power AI systems. Pocock argues Australia is falling behind on regulating AI risks while giving the industry a free pass on infrastructure costs. This is part of a broader global conversation about who pays for AI's energy footprint and how governments protect citizens from AI harms.

stories.title: GPT vs Claude vs Gemini: 2024 benchmark results released
stories.why_it_matters: Head-to-head benchmark results comparing OpenAI's GPT models, Anthropic's Claude, and Google's Gemini have been released. These tests measure things like reasoning, coding, creative writing, and factual accuracy across the leading AI models. For anyone deciding which AI tool to use — or which company to back as an investor — benchmark results like these are the scorecard that matters.

stories.title: Ant Group's AI app open-sources medical and health AI model family
stories.why_it_matters: Ant Group — the Chinese fintech giant behind Alipay — has open-sourced its family of medical and health AI models through its Afu app. Open-sourcing means anyone can download, use, and build on these models for free. In practical terms, this could accelerate AI-powered health tools worldwide — think symptom checkers, drug interaction alerts, or clinical decision support — while also intensifying competition with US-based AI health startups.

stories.title: US Governors call for aligned AI regulation across states
stories.why_it_matters: US state Governors are pushing for a unified, nationally-aligned approach to AI regulation rather than a patchwork of different rules in each state. The concern is that 50 different sets of AI laws creates confusion for businesses and leaves gaps that bad actors can exploit. For companies like Microsoft and Google — both in your portfolio — clearer and consistent regulation is generally better for business planning.

stories.title: GLM-4.5 launches: China's answer to GPT-4 is here
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese AI lab Zhipu AI has launched GLM-4.5, one of the most capable Chinese-made large language models to date. It's being positioned as a direct competitor to GPT-4 and Claude, with API access available for developers. This matters because it shows the AI race isn't just a US-vs-US competition — Chinese labs are closing the gap rapidly, which will intensify pressure on US AI companies to keep innovating.

sport.summary: NRL Grand Final result is in — the Roosters edged the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. Jannik Sinner faces knee surgery and could miss the Australian Open. The AFL draft season is producing some surprises. And Carlos Alcaraz has cemented his place among tennis's all-time greats.

stories.title: Roosters win NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters claimed the 2026 NRL premiership in a heart-stopping one-point win over the Newcastle Knights — 19 to 18 — at Accor Stadium on Sunday night. It was the kind of Grand Final you couldn't script: one point separating the teams at the final whistle. The Roosters continue their status as one of the game's elite clubs, while for Knights fans it's a heartbreaking near-miss.

stories.title: Sam Walker makes shock decision on his future
stories.why_it_matters: Sydney Roosters halfback Sam Walker has made a shock decision about his playing future — the details aren't fully available, but the timing (just after the Grand Final) makes this significant news for one of the NRL's most talented young playmakers. Walker was a key part of the Roosters' premiership campaign.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner faces knee surgery — Australian Open in doubt
stories.why_it_matters: World number one Jannik Sinner is set to undergo surgery on his right knee and could be sidelined until Wimbledon — meaning he'd almost certainly miss the Australian Open in January. Sinner has been the dominant force in men's tennis this year, and his absence from the AO would blow the draw wide open. Carlos Alcaraz, fresh off his historic ATP Finals win, would become the clear favourite.

stories.title: Alcaraz joins Agassi, Federer and Djokovic — wins all four Slams and ATP Finals
stories.why_it_matters: Carlos Alcaraz has become only the fourth man in tennis history to win all four Grand Slams and the ATP Finals, joining Andre Agassi, Roger Federer, and Novak Djokovic in an exclusive club. At 23, he's already one of the greatest players the sport has ever seen. With Sinner now facing surgery, Alcaraz looks set to dominate the 2027 season.

stories.title: AFL Draft: Essendon signs 209cm giant, nine players get rookie lifelines
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL's supplemental draft and rookie list movements have thrown up some surprises — Essendon signed a 209cm ruckman, and nine players across the competition received rookie lifelines, keeping their AFL careers alive for another season. A former North Melbourne player also got an unexpected second chance at a new club. The official AFL Draft is coming up and clubs are jostling for position.
